channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You ignore the math when certainty is on the table.
item.description: The 'pseudocertainty' effect explains why people choose a certain, smaller gain over a larger, statistically superior gamble.

item.title: You change your mind when you cannot use tools.
item.description: In a 1945 study, participants failed to solve problems because they could not stop seeing an object's 'intended' use.

item.title: You see motion in lights that stay perfectly still.
item.description: The autokinetic effect was first systematically applied in psychology by Muzafer Sherif in 1935 to study social norms, though the phenomenon was documented by astronomers much earlier.

item.title: You judge powerful people based on their physical height.
item.description: Research shows that participants consistently associate power-related concepts like 'leader' or 'dominant' with items placed at the top of a screen.

item.title: It is physically harder to look back at things.
item.description: Inhibition of return typically manifests when the interval between a stimulus cue and a target exceeds approximately 300 milliseconds.

item.title: Your attention is limited to one object.
item.description: When you are highly focused on a specific task, you may experience 'inattentional blindness,' where you fail to notice unexpected stimuli in your visual field.

item.title: You assume the person next to you is fine.
item.description: The 'pluralistic ignorance' effect leads individuals to believe they are the only ones struggling while everyone else appears satisfied.

item.title: You overestimate your control over random outcomes.
item.description: When participants in a 1975 study were asked to pick a card, they were more confident of winning if they picked it themselves.

item.title: You prioritize small gains over large rewards.
item.description: The 'present bias' is an economic model describing the tendency to value smaller, immediate rewards over larger, delayed ones.

item.title: You believe your future self is a stranger.
item.description: Neuroimaging studies indicate that, for individuals with low future-self continuity, the brain processes the future self similarly to how it processes other people, with a notable reduction in mPFC activation compared to the present self.

item.title: Your brain saves energy by ignoring repetition.
item.description: Neural activity in the sensory cortex often shows a statistically significant decrease on average when an image is repeated compared to its initial presentation.

item.title: You struggle to change your mind despite evidence.
item.description: Belief persistence describes the psychological tendency to maintain an initial belief even after the evidence supporting it is proven false.

item.title: You perform differently when the task requires effort.
item.description: The effort-accuracy trade-off shows that you adjust your cognitive effort based on how much accuracy you believe the task requires.

item.title: You categorize people before you know their names.
item.description: The social categorization process begins almost instantly, shifting your perception of an individual based on their group identity.

item.title: You avoid thinking deeply even when you could.
item.description: Cognitive reflection is the tendency to override an intuitive, incorrect response in favor of a more deliberate, accurate one.

item.title: You have a limit to your internal mental voice.
item.description: The phonological loop was introduced as a model component by Baddeley and Hitch in 1974, but the finding that its capacity is limited by rehearsal/pronunciation time was demonstrated by Baddeley in 1975.

item.title: Your mood at this moment dictates your life evaluation.
item.description: The mood-as-information hypothesis suggests that you use your current affective state as a heuristic to judge your life satisfaction.

item.title: Your best decisions happen when you stop thinking hard.
item.description: A 2006 study by Dijksterhuis proposed that complex decisions are made more effectively when distracted, though these findings have faced extensive challenges in replication.

item.title: Anxiety changes what you pay attention to in conversation.
item.description: Attentional control theory suggests that anxiety impairs your ability to shift attention away from task-irrelevant stimuli.

item.title: You can deliberately choose to forget useless information.
item.description: Directed forgetting shows that you can reduce the accessibility of specific information when given a signal to do so.

item.title: Holding a warm cup changes your impression of people.
item.description: A 2008 study suggested that holding a warm beverage might influence social perception, but this finding has failed to replicate in larger, independent studies.

item.title: You only notice how much you have when it disappears.
item.description: The adaptation-level phenomenon suggests that people experience significant hedonic adaptation, but individuals often only partially return to their prior happiness baseline after major life changes.

item.title: Your brain treats numbers as physical space.
item.description: The SNARC effect reveals that humans associate smaller numbers with the left side of space and larger numbers with the right.

item.title: You consistently underestimate your own internal narrative.
item.description: The narrative fallacy describes your tendency to force complex, random events into simple, cause-and-effect stories.

item.title: You judge people by your own hidden assumptions.
item.description: The trait-inference task demonstrates that you spontaneously label others with personality traits within milliseconds of seeing a face.

item.title: You avoid information that makes you feel bad.
item.description: The ostrich effect refers to the tendency for individuals to avoid information that might be negative or disappointing, such as checking investment portfolios during market downturns.

item.title: You value things more if you helped make them.
item.description: The IKEA effect demonstrates that personal labor increases the perceived value of an object, provided that the labor results in the successful completion of the task.

item.title: You blame the person, not the situation.
item.description: The correspondence bias describes your tendency to infer a person's character from their behavior while ignoring situational pressures.

item.title: Your memory stores only the gist of experiences.
item.description: Leveling and sharpening causes you to omit details while exaggerating specific core elements when recalling a story or event.

item.title: You struggle to change a rule once established.
item.description: Mental set, or the Einstellung effect, happens when you become fixated on a single approach and fail to see simpler, alternative solutions.

item.title: You ignore information that disagrees with your prior beliefs.
item.description: The disconfirmation bias leads you to spend more cognitive effort scrutinizing and attacking evidence that contradicts your existing opinions.

item.title: Your brain processes familiar words faster than uncommon ones.
item.description: The word-frequency effect shows that you recognize high-frequency words significantly faster than words you encounter rarely.

item.title: Your memory changes every time you recall it.
item.description: Memory reconsolidation is a process where retrieved memories can become labile and subject to modification under specific boundary conditions, such as prediction error.

item.title: Darkness changes the way you think.
item.description: A 2013 study found that dimmed ambient lighting significantly boosts creative performance compared to bright light settings.

item.title: Sometimes you choose ignorance over useful information.
item.description: A 2010 review found that individuals intentionally avoid available information if they believe that data will threaten their current emotional state.

item.title: You are more likely to lie when the incentive is small.
item.description: Research indicates that the level of dishonesty is largely independent of the magnitude of the reward.

item.title: You feel more confident in a decision after it is made.
item.description: Choice-supportive bias drives the brain to emphasize the positives of a chosen option and ignore its drawbacks post-selection.

item.title: Your brain predicts what you see before you actually see it.
item.description: The predictive processing model suggests your brain creates a mental model of reality and updates it with sensory error signals.

item.title: Your brain reconstructs memories to fit a coherent narrative structure.
item.description: Bartlett demonstrated that memory is a reconstructive process influenced by cultural schemas.

item.title: You naturally prefer effortful thinking over simple, automated shortcuts.
item.description: The 'need for cognition' trait measures a person's intrinsic tendency to engage in and enjoy effortful mental exertion.

item.title: Performing a simple ritual lowers your anxiety before high-stakes tasks.
item.description: Research shows that simple, repetitive ritualistic behaviors can reduce physiological distress before a performance, particularly for those experiencing high levels of performance anxiety.

item.title: Your brain creates meaning out of literal noise.
item.description: Klaus Conrad originally coined 'apophenia' in 1958 to describe a clinical symptom of the early stages of schizophrenia, not a general human cognitive tendency.

item.title: You fear losing more than you value gaining.
item.description: Prospect theory demonstrates that losses are weighted more heavily than equivalent gains.

item.title: You are less rational when you are hungry.
item.description: The theory that self-control is a limited metabolic resource fueled by blood glucose has been widely challenged and failed to replicate in large-scale studies.

item.title: Your brain ignores details that complicate your narrative.
item.description: The 'Schema-Consistent Bias' causes you to recall information that fits your existing framework while forgetting incongruent facts.

item.title: Your brain prefers simple patterns over complex reality.
item.description: The 'Representativeness Heuristic' leads you to judge the probability of an event by how much it resembles your mental prototype.

item.title: You actively block your own goals to focus.
item.description: Goal shielding is the process where the activation of a target goal inhibits the accessibility of competing goals.

item.title: Your brain hallucinates words you did not hear.
item.description: In the phonemic restoration effect, listeners report hearing a missing phoneme in a word if the gap is replaced by a non-speech sound.

item.title: You vividly remember events that never happened.
item.description: In a 1995 study, 25% of participants formed false memories of being lost in a shopping mall after being prompted with a narrative.

item.title: You categorize people to save your brain energy.
item.description: A 1994 study demonstrated that stereotypes act as cognitive energy-saving devices, allowing people to conserve cognitive resources during complex tasks.
